reading.body:
Amazon Web Services recorded $717 billion in revenue in 2025 while operating two major AI product lines: SageMaker for full-stack ML lifecycle management and Bedrock for managed foundation model access.

AWS sits at the intersection of compute supply and AI demand. SageMaker's architecture—unified data lakes, model monitoring, bias detection, and governance tools—reflects the infrastructure required to run production AI at scale. Bedrock's API model with VPC support and IAM integration suggests AWS is positioning itself as the managed layer between foundation models and enterprise users who want isolation and control. Both products point to a company treating AI not as a feature but as a platform business spanning data, compute, and model serving.

The scale here matters for power and buildings. A $717 billion revenue company in cloud services operates data centers globally to deliver these products. The fact that SageMaker includes toxicity detection, guardrails, and data lineage tracking indicates AWS is building compliance and observability into the compute layer itself. This is not decorative. As regulatory exposure grows, the infrastructure provider that bakes governance into the platform gains advantage over those that bolt it on later.

The data does not specify AWS's capital spending, energy consumption, or data center locations. It does not break out AI revenue from total AWS revenue or show whether SageMaker and Bedrock are growing faster than legacy services. It does not name which foundation models Bedrock serves or how much compute AWS allocates to these two products versus others.

profile_text.body:
Amazon Web Services presents Amazon SageMaker as the center for data, analytics, and AI, an integrated environment for building analytics and AI on a single platform. The site describes the next generation of SageMaker as bringing together AWS machine learning and analytics capabilities with unified access to data, including SageMaker Unified Studio, model development tools in SageMaker AI such as HyperPod, JumpStart, and MLOps, and Amazon Q Developer, which the company describes as the most capable generative AI assistant for software development. It also describes a lakehouse architecture across Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift, Apache Iceberg-compatible tools, zero-ETL integrations, governance through Amazon SageMaker Catalog, and open source frameworks on Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue. Customer quotes on the page, from an automotive company and from Carrier, describe unifying and governing data across business units and accelerating lakehouse work.

Two products are tracked for the company. Amazon SageMaker is listed for full ML lifecycle management, model monitoring, bias detection, and explainability tools. AWS Bedrock is listed as a managed foundation model API service with IAM integration, VPC support, model evaluation tools, and AgentCore for agent orchestration. The site frames SageMaker as secure by design, with governance across the data and AI lifecycle, including data classification, toxicity detection, guardrails, and responsible AI policies.

The company is recorded as a for-profit public company founded in 1994, headquartered in Seattle, Washington, and trading as AMZN, with a CIK of 0001018724. Its most recent revenue figure is $716,924,000,000 for the period ending 2025-12-31, reported on Form 10-K. On litigation, the record lists the case Haugland v. Anthropic PBC in the District Court, D. Delaware, and 107 cases in Washington.
